fieldMarks: Second-largest skink in the account, up to 324 mm; males become uniform brown and lose their stripes.
Breeding-season males have a greatly enlarged orange to red head.
Juveniles brown to black with five to seven white to light-orange stripes and a bright blue tail; adult females keep some striping but lose the blue tail.
Five labial scales around the mouth (five-lined skinks have four).
behavior: Diurnal and solitary; mainly arboreal but often hunts and nests on the ground; sun themselves on snags and stumps.
Eats insects, arachnids, mollusks, isopods, rodents and smaller reptiles including juveniles of its own species, hunting by sight and tongue-flicking.
Hibernates October-March in northern parts of range; males are territorial in the breeding season; females guard eggs in rotting stumps or dead trees.
habitat: Open forests and woodland edges, hammocks and cypress heads in Florida, swamps and barrier islands; uses tree hollows and old woodpecker holes, and large live oaks on coastal islands.
range: Central and eastern United States, from Pennsylvania to Florida and Indiana to Texas. Not in Canada.
